A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that helps websites load faster no matter where a visitor happens to be. Normally, every request for a photo, video, or webpage travels all the way back to a single origin server, the original computer where that website's files are permanently stored. If that server sits far away, loading feels slow. A CDN solves this by keeping copies of popular files in many edge locations, which are smaller computers positioned closer to everyday people in different regions. When someone requests a file and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, and it means the file arrives almost instantly, without a long trip back to the origin. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep copies of the most popular books, so borrowers no longer need to travel to one distant central library every time. Only when a file is missing locally does the request continue back to the origin server to fetch it, after which nearby locations often store a copy for next time. This quiet system speeds up streaming, shopping, and browsing while easing pressure on the original server.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It's the ultimate source when no nearby copy exists |
| Edge location | A smaller server placed close to everyday users | It shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | A successful delivery from a saved nearby copy | It makes loading much faster and more reliable |
| CDN | A network linking origin servers and edge locations | It spreads traffic and prevents slowdowns during heavy demand |
